cards.front: Scientists sort every species into eight main levels, nested like boxes, from {{c1::domain}}, the most general, to species, the most specific.
cards.quote: Scientists sort every species into eight main levels, nested like boxes, from domain, the most general, to species, the most specific.

cards.front: Name the eight main levels of classification, from most general to most specific.
cards.back: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
cards.quote: The eight main levels, from most general to most specific, are domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species.
cards.section: Explain: eight boxes, from general to specific

cards.front: According to the film, what is the test for a species?
cards.back: Similar organisms that can mate in nature and have young that can also reproduce (a useful rule for many sexually reproducing organisms, with limits).
cards.quote: similar organisms that can mate in nature and have young that can also reproduce, is a useful rule for many organisms that reproduce with sex cells
cards.section: Explain: one name for each species

cards.front: The species test (can mate in nature and have young that can reproduce) has two limits. What are they?
cards.back: It cannot be used for organisms that reproduce without sex, such as many bacteria. And some different species do sometimes mate in nature.
cards.quote: It cannot be used for organisms that reproduce without sex, such as many bacteria.
cards.section: Explain: one name for each species

cards.front: Giving each species one two-part scientific name is called {{c1::binomial nomenclature}}.
cards.quote: one two-part name for each species, is called binomial nomenclature
cards.section: Explain: one name for each species

cards.front: In a two-part scientific name, what does each word tell you?
cards.back: The first word is the genus, a small group of closely related species. The second word names one species in that genus.
cards.why: One genus can hold several species, so the genus name alone is not enough.
cards.quote: The first word is the genus, a small group of closely related species, so one genus can hold several species.
cards.section: Explain: one name for each species

cards.front: The black vulture is in genus Coragyps, and the second word of its name is atratus. Write its scientific name the way you would by hand.
cards.back: Coragyps atratus, with both words underlined.
cards.quote: The black vulture's full name is Coragyps atratus.
cards.section: Explain: one name for each species

cards.front: Why can the word "buzzard" cause a mix-up between Virginia and Britain, and how does a scientific name fix it?
cards.back: In Virginia some people call vultures buzzards; in Britain a buzzard is a hawk. A scientific name is the same in every country, so everyone knows which bird is meant.
cards.quote: In Virginia, some people call vultures buzzards. In Britain, a buzzard is a hawk.

cards.front: The science of naming and classifying living things is {{c1::taxonomy}}.
cards.quote: The science of naming and classifying living things is taxonomy.
cards.section: Explain: eight boxes, from general to specific

cards.front: There are three domains of life: Eukarya, Archaea and Bacteria. How are the cells of Archaea and Bacteria different from those of Eukarya?
cards.back: The cells of Archaea and Bacteria have no nucleus.
cards.quote: the other two domains are Archaea and Bacteria, whose cells have no nucleus.
cards.section: Explain: eight boxes, from general to specific

cards.front: What evidence do scientists use to decide where the walls between classification groups go, and can a wall move?
cards.back: They compare body parts, what organisms do, and DNA. Yes: new evidence can move a wall.
cards.quote: Scientists place the walls by comparing body parts, what organisms do, and DNA
cards.section: Explain: eight boxes, from general to specific

cards.front: In the ITIS database, the turkey vulture and red-tailed hawk share 5 boxes, down to order Accipitriformes. Another bird checklist gives the New World vultures their own order, Cathartiformes. Under that checklist, do the two birds share more boxes or fewer?
cards.back: Fewer: 4, down to class Aves. The order box now holds the vultures alone, so the hawk leaves one box sooner.
cards.why: The birds did not change; one wall moved. A count of shared boxes belongs to one classification at one time.
cards.quote: Another bird checklist, from the American Ornithological Society, gives the New World vultures their own order, Cathartiformes.
cards.section: Explain: eight boxes, from general to specific

cards.front: What is a dichotomous key?
cards.back: A list of two-choice questions that leads to the name of an organism.
cards.quote: A dichotomous key is a list of two-choice questions that leads to a name.

cards.front: An animal key asks, in order: fins (brook trout)? Jointed legs (blue crab)? A shell of two hinged halves (eastern oyster)? Five-part arms (sea star)? Ring-like segments (earthworm)? Last: fixed in place with holes (sponge), or a swimming bell with tentacles (sea nettle)? A garden snail has no fins, no jointed legs and one shell. Where does it end up?
cards.back: Nowhere. Its one shell is not two hinged halves, it has no five-part arms or segments, and it is neither a sponge nor a swimming bell.
cards.why: A key works only for the organisms built into it.
cards.quote: A key works only for the organisms built into it.

cards.front: A plant key: Step 1, woody twig (go to 2) or no woody twig (go to 3). Step 2: needles in bundles with cones (loblolly pine), or broad leaves with four showy bracts (flowering dogwood). Step 3: large fronds with spore cases (fern), or a tiny leafy plant with a capsule on a thin stalk (moss). A plant has no woody twig and large fronds with spore cases. What is it?
cards.back: A fern: no woody twig sends you to step 3, and large fronds with spore cases give fern.
cards.quote: Large fronds with spore cases: fern.

cards.front: A class reorders the questions in a dichotomous key. The brook trout's neighbors in the key change, but every student still reaches the right names. Does this change how closely the trout is related to its new neighbors?
cards.back: No. Both orders find the names, so both keys work, but neighbors in a key are not shown to be related.
cards.why: A key is a tool for finding names. How closely organisms are grouped comes from the boxes of classification they share.
cards.quote: It finds the name, but the order of its questions does not show how living things are grouped.

cards.front: A table lists ten organisms. Six of them (two vultures, a hawk, a buzzard, a cardinal and a brook trout) are in phylum Chordata. What percent of the table is in Chordata?
cards.back: 6 of 10 organisms is 60 out of 100, so 60 percent.
cards.quote: How many of the ten organisms are in phylum Chordata? What percent of the table is that?

cards.front: In the ITIS database, the turkey vulture is in domain Eukarya, Animalia, Chordata, Aves, order Accipitriformes, family Cathartidae. The common buzzard and red-tailed hawk are both in Eukarya, Animalia, Chordata, Aves, Accipitriformes, family Accipitridae. Which bird is grouped closer to the turkey vulture?
cards.back: Neither: it is a tie. Each shares 5 levels with the turkey vulture, down to order Accipitriformes.
cards.why: Being called a buzzard does not move a bird closer. Only shared boxes count.
cards.quote: Each shares 5 levels with the turkey vulture, down to order Accipitriformes.

cards.front: ITIS puts the brook trout in class Teleostei, while many books use the larger group Actinopterygii. A student says counting the boxes the trout shares with another fish tells how long ago they had a common ancestor. Is the student right?
cards.back: No. A count of shared boxes ranks grouping in one classification only, and books can draw the walls differently. It does not tell how long ago the most recent common ancestor lived.
cards.quote: A count of shared boxes ranks grouping in one classification; it does not tell how long ago the organisms' most recent common ancestor lived.

cards.front: Plan a fair test with picture cards: does the order of questions in a dichotomous key change how many organisms people name correctly?
cards.back: Independent variable: question order (key 1 or key 2, same questions). Dependent: correct names out of 10 cards, and time. Constants: same cards, same time limit, no help. Control: key 1. At least 10 classmates per key; report means.
cards.why: Use pictures, not live or wild-caught animals.
cards.quote: Independent variable: the order of the questions (key 1 or key 2, same questions).
